The story changed here

Unexpected Findings That Changed the Story

The clusters were useful—but the most valuable moments came when the data contradicted the simple story. Two patterns shifted the analysis from describing users to identifying practical intervention points.

Finding 01 · Context hiding in plain sight
Device preference unexpectedly mapped onto behavioral profiles.
Evidence
  • C1 repeatedly favored tablet; C2 was predominantly mobile.
  • C3 combined TV, long-form content, and multi-device behavior.
  • C4 was primarily desktop-based.
  • Those device patterns remained stable across weeks.
Interpretation

Device choice appeared to reflect the context in which exercise fit into a user’s life—structured at-home routines, short mobile sessions, immersive TV workouts, or desktop-based exploration.

Business Use

Preferred device could serve as an early, low-cost signal for cold-start segmentation—not as a cluster label, but as a starting hypothesis. TSS could personalize onboarding, content recommendations, and initial messaging, then refine the segment as behavioral history develops.

Finding 02 · The quiet majority
The least active group held the greatest activation potential.
More than half of usersHighest challenge upliftPost-challenge retention in the low-60% range
Evidence

C2 was the largest segment—representing more than half of users—and had the lowest total viewing and consistency. Yet it responded most strongly during the challenge. The sharpest gap appeared afterward, when retention settled in the low-60% range.

Interpretation

The challenge proved that these users were reachable. Their drop-off came when temporary motivation ended without a continuing routine to carry it forward.

Business Use · Build a post-challenge bridge
Immediate follow-upMobile-first quickiesShort repeat challengesConsistency reminders

Cluster 2 is highly responsive to activation. The retention opportunity lies in helping that initial response develop into a repeatable habit.

Learning analytics · Team project

What student behavior can—and cannot—predict

Using event-level data from Carnegie Learning’s MATHia platform, our team investigated whether patterns inside an online math tutor could predict three different outcomes: math knowledge, metacognition, and motivation.

Python / RXGBoostFeature engineeringRepeated train-test splitsCross-validationModel interpretation

Research question

Can the way a student works through problems reveal not only what they learn, but also how they monitor learning and sustain motivation?

Behavioral features

We summarized session frequency, time and actions per workspace, hint timing, help intensity, error correction, mastery progress, and task completion.

Model design

We trained separate XGBoost models because each outcome had a different measurement structure. Math knowledge used regression; metacognition and motivation used ordinal classification.

Validation

Cross-validation guided model complexity and early stopping. Repeated train-test splits tested whether the psychological-outcome results were stable or dependent on a lucky split.

What worked

Behavioral logs carried a strong signal for later math performance. In-progress performance, persistence, and help use gave the model useful information about learning.

What did not

The same logs were far less informative for metacognition and motivation. That inconclusive result suggested that internal states cannot be recovered reliably from clicks alone.

Practical direction

A math-performance model could support early educator alerts. Psychological outcomes need richer evidence, such as short self-reports or measures designed to capture affect and cognition directly.

Behavioral observation · Platform hint use

A hint click was not a single story

At first, opening a hint immediately could look like low persistence. The learning outcomes told a more complicated story: when students used the hint—and what happened afterward—revealed two meaningfully different patterns.

Pattern 01 · Quick hint use

A short-term lift, followed by a transfer gap

Students who opened question-specific hints quickly often performed well on short quizzes. For concept-focused questions—such as identifying a definition, term, or principle—the platform hint could work as a just-in-time scaffold, helping them revisit the relevant idea while it was still in context.

The story changed on broader assessments.

Their advantage faded when problems required multi-step reasoning or independent application. The pattern suggested that quick hints could strengthen conceptual recall without necessarily building the same depth of transfer. These students did not simply need “more help”; they needed practice moving from recognizing a concept to applying it without a scaffold.

Pattern 02 · Hint before a first attempt

When getting started was the real barrier

A second group opened the platform hint before making any attempt. Unlike the first group, these students performed below average on both short quizzes and larger exams.

That timing changed the meaning of the click.

Rather than using the hint to refresh a specific concept, they may have been unsure how to enter the problem at all. This pattern pointed toward gaps in foundational understanding or study approach—and a stronger case for teacher follow-up, guided review, and help identifying the first productive step.

The practical lesson: quick hint use may represent strategic use of a scaffold, while a hint opened before any attempt may signal difficulty initiating the task. Treating both clicks as the same behavior would hide the students who need a different kind of support.

Three product ideas generated from the observation

01 · Progressive hints

Break a complete solution into step-by-step guidance. Start with a brief reminder or directional cue, then reveal additional support only when needed.

02 · Hint cooldown

Add a short pause between successive hint reveals or attempts so students have time to process the current guidance and try the next step themselves.

03 · Concept resurfacing

Reintroduce the same underlying concept later in a different question, giving students another opportunity to retrieve and apply it without relying on the original hint.

Self-directed project · In progress

E-commerce Analytics Copilot

I am building a narrow, testable analytics assistant for e-commerce conversion questions using obfuscated GA4 sample data. The project connects reproducible SQL, a shared metric layer, and a guarded natural-language-to-SQL workflow.

BigQuerySQLGA4 event dataMetric designExperiment designLLM evaluation

A strict analytical spine

The analysis follows an ordered session funnel so each step is counted only after the preceding eligible event. Device, acquisition context, and product category are examined without treating descriptive differences as causal.

view_itemadd_to_cartbegin_checkoutpurchase

Guardrails before generation

The planned copilot is deliberately constrained to read-only SQL, approved public tables and fields, a fixed analysis window, and visible SQL validation before execution.

From observation to a testable decision

A descriptive funnel opportunity will inform a proposed randomized experiment with a defined population, primary metric, guardrails, minimum detectable effect, sample-size plan, and decision rule. No experiment result or causal lift is claimed.

Evaluation as part of the product

The prototype will be checked against manually validated SQL for supported questions and will also be tested on requests it should clarify or refuse. The goal is bounded analytical reliability—not a general-purpose data assistant.
